title: MT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: Free 30-Question Mock Exam
metaDescription: Free MT Level II mock exam: 30 original magnetic particle testing questions with answers on field direction, equipment checks, interpretation and demag.
h1: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) Level II Practice Questions
intro: These 30 questions are original study questions written by Atlantis NDT for technicians preparing for Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) Level II. They are not ASNT examination questions and do not reproduce any certification exam.

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition), the employer certifies Level II personnel after general, specific and practical examinations set out in its written practice. ASNT also offers central ASNT NDT Level II examinations (general and method exams), and employers still carry out the vision, practical and job-specific examinations. This set is pitched at what a Level II must do: choose and verify the magnetizing technique, carry out the examination, interpret and evaluate indications against a procedure, and report the results.

The questions cover magnetism principles, current types and field direction, equipment and particle checks, technique control, interpretation, demagnetization and safety. Atlantis NDT runs NDT training year-round, with theory online and practicals in its Practical NDT simulator or in person at the client's own facility.
howToUse: Answer each question before opening the explanation, and note the topic of every question you miss.
For scenario questions, decide the field direction or system check you would use at the bench before reading the options.
Check code references against the edition your procedures and written practice actually use, since requirements can change between editions.
Study your weakest topics, then retake the full set a few days later without notes.

questions.q: Which of these materials can be examined by magnetic particle testing?
options: Austenitic stainless steel (type 316)
Aluminum alloy
Copper
Carbon steel
questions.explanation: MT needs a ferromagnetic material that can be strongly magnetized, such as carbon and low-alloy steel. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper are not ferromagnetic, so penetrant or eddy current testing is used instead.

questions.q: Why do magnetic particles collect at a surface crack in a magnetized part?
options: The crack distorts the field and creates a flux leakage field at the surface that attracts the particles
The particles are drawn into the crack by capillary action
The crack carries more current than the surrounding metal
The particles are electrostatically charged by the magnetizing current
questions.explanation: A discontinuity across the flux path forces some flux out of the part, forming poles at the crack edges, and this leakage field holds the particles. Capillary action is the penetrant testing mechanism, not MT.

questions.q: Which property describes a material's ability to retain magnetism after the magnetizing force is removed?
options: Permeability
Retentivity
Reluctance
Conductivity
questions.explanation: Retentivity is the ability to retain residual magnetism. Permeability is the ease with which a material is magnetized, and reluctance is the opposition to magnetic flux.

questions.q: A ferromagnetic material with a wide hysteresis loop typically:
options: Has low retentivity and is easy to demagnetize
Has high permeability and very little residual magnetism
Has high coercive force and is harder to demagnetize
Cannot be magnetized with direct current
questions.explanation: A wide loop indicates a magnetically hard material, such as hardened steel, with high retentivity and high coercive force, so more effort is needed to demagnetize it. Soft, low-carbon steels show narrow loops and high permeability.

questions.q: For the best chance of detecting a discontinuity, how should the magnetic field be oriented relative to it?
options: Parallel to the discontinuity
Perpendicular to the discontinuity
At about 10° to the discontinuity
Orientation does not matter
questions.explanation: The leakage field is strongest when the flux crosses the discontinuity at right angles, while a discontinuity parallel to the field produces little or no leakage. This is why each area is examined with two fields at approximately 90° to each other.

questions.q: Which current type gives the best sensitivity to discontinuities lying slightly below the surface?
options: Alternating current (AC)
High-frequency alternating current
Direct current, including rectified current such as half-wave DC
Current type has no effect on how deep the field reaches
questions.explanation: AC is concentrated near the surface by the skin effect, which suits surface-breaking cracks. DC and rectified currents magnetize deeper into the part and so give better sensitivity to near-surface discontinuities.

questions.q: Current passed end to end through a bar (a head shot) produces which field, and which discontinuities does it detect best?
options: A longitudinal field; transverse discontinuities
A circular field; discontinuities parallel to the bar's long axis
A circular field; discontinuities perpendicular to the long axis
No field inside the bar; only end-face discontinuities
questions.explanation: Current flowing along the bar creates a circular field around its axis, which crosses longitudinal discontinuities at right angles. Transverse discontinuities need a longitudinal field, for example from a coil.

questions.q: A long bar is magnetized in an encircling coil. Which discontinuities are best detected?
options: Transverse discontinuities, perpendicular to the bar's axis
Longitudinal discontinuities, parallel to the bar's axis
Only discontinuities on the end faces
Only subsurface laminations
questions.explanation: A coil produces a longitudinal field along the bar's axis, which crosses transverse discontinuities. Longitudinal discontinuities lie parallel to this field and give little leakage.

questions.q: The inside surface of a steel tube must be examined for longitudinal cracks. Which technique is most suitable?
options: A head shot with current passed through the tube wall
An encircling coil
A central conductor (threader bar) passed through the bore
A permanent magnet on the outside surface
questions.explanation: Current through a central conductor creates a circular field in the tube wall at both the inside and outside surfaces, crossing longitudinal cracks. With a head shot through a hollow part, the field at the inside surface is essentially zero.

questions.q: Using the right-hand rule for a straight conductor, if the thumb points in the direction of conventional current flow, the curled fingers show:
options: The direction of particle movement
The direction of a longitudinal field along the conductor
The direction of current induced in the part
The direction of the circular magnetic field around the conductor
questions.explanation: With the conductor grasped and the thumb along the current, the fingers curl in the direction of the circular field. Inspectors use this to predict field direction for head shots, central conductors and prods.

questions.q: When using prods, which discontinuities are best detected, and what is a key risk?
options: Discontinuities parallel to the line joining the prods; arc burns at the contact points
Discontinuities perpendicular to the line joining the prods; demagnetization of the part
Only subsurface discontinuities; overheating of the particles
Discontinuities in any direction from one placement; no particular risk
questions.explanation: Current flows between the prod tips, producing a circular field that crosses discontinuities lying along the current path. Poor contact, or energizing before firm contact, can cause arc burns that may be unacceptable on finished or hardenable surfaces.
questions.ref: General MT principle; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 7

questions.q: With an electromagnetic yoke, a discontinuity is best detected when it lies:
options: Parallel to the line joining the poles
Directly under one pole
Between the poles and perpendicular to the line joining them
Outside the area between the poles
questions.explanation: A yoke produces a longitudinal field running from pole to pole, so discontinuities lying across that line produce the strongest leakage. The yoke is then repositioned at about 90° to cover the other orientation.

questions.q: Under ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709, what minimum lifting power must an AC electromagnetic yoke have at the maximum pole spacing that will be used?
options: 25 lb (11 kg)
40 lb (18 kg)
50 lb (23 kg)
questions.explanation: AC yokes must lift at least 10 lb (4.5 kg), and DC or permanent-magnet yokes at least 40 lb (18 kg), at the maximum pole spacing that will be used. The check is made with a test weight at the intervals the code or procedure sets.
questions.ref: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 7; ASTM E709

questions.q: What is an artificial flaw shim used for in MT?
options: To measure the concentration of the wet particle bath
To show that the field at the surface is adequate in strength and direction to reveal a fine discontinuity
To demagnetize small parts
To measure UV-A intensity at the surface
questions.explanation: A shim carries a fine artificial notch; fixed notch-side to the surface, a clear indication shows the field and technique can reveal a discontinuity in that orientation. Pie-shaped indicators are mainly used to show field direction, and bath concentration is checked by a settling test.
questions.ref: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 7; ASTM E1444

questions.q: How is the concentration of a wet magnetic particle bath normally checked?
options: With a hydrometer
With a viscosity cup
With a UV-A meter
By a settling test in a pear-shaped centrifuge tube
questions.explanation: A measured sample is left to settle for the time the standard sets, and the settled volume is read and compared with the procedure limits. The settled sample is also checked for contamination.

questions.q: Which particle type generally gives the highest sensitivity to fine surface cracks?
options: Dry visible powder
Wet fluorescent particles
Coarse dry powder applied by hand
Dry red powder on a hot surface
questions.explanation: Small fluorescent particles in a liquid carrier are highly mobile, and a bright indication against a dark background is easy to see. Dry powder is better suited to rough surfaces and near-surface discontinuities with rectified current.

questions.q: In the wet continuous method, when are the particles applied?
options: Only after the current has been switched off, using the residual field
Before the part is magnetized, with the bath then allowed to dry
While the magnetizing force is present, so the particles collect in the presence of the field
After the part has been demagnetized
questions.explanation: In the continuous method the bath is applied so the particles are still mobile while the magnetizing current is on, and the flow is stopped as the final shot is applied so indications are not washed away. Applying particles after the current is off is the residual method.

questions.q: A Level II must look for near-surface lack of fusion in a rough multipass weld using portable equipment. Which combination is generally most effective?
options: AC with wet fluorescent particles
Half-wave rectified DC with dry powder
A permanent magnet with wet visible particles
An AC coil with no particles, reading a field meter
questions.explanation: Rectified current magnetizes below the surface, and the pulsating field helps dry powder move toward leakage fields on rough surfaces. AC with wet fluorescent particles is the better choice for fine surface-breaking cracks.

questions.q: Why should thick paint or coatings normally be removed before MT?
options: They increase the distance between the leakage field and the particles, reducing sensitivity
They make the part non-magnetic
They increase the flux density in the part
They prevent demagnetization
questions.explanation: Leakage fields weaken quickly with distance from the discontinuity, so a thick coating can hide fine cracks. Thin coatings may be left only where the procedure has been shown to detect the required discontinuities through them.
questions.ref: General MT principle; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 7

questions.q: Which viewing conditions are required when inspecting with fluorescent magnetic particles?
options: Bright white light at the surface, with no UV-A source
A UV-C lamp to make the particles brighter
A polarizing filter over the inspector's eyes
A darkened area, a UV-A source and verification of UV-A intensity at the examination surface with a meter
questions.explanation: Fluorescent indications are viewed under UV-A in reduced ambient light, with UV-A intensity and ambient light checked against the procedure limits and the inspector's eyes allowed to adapt to the dark. UV-C is hazardous and is not used.
questions.ref: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 7; ASTM E709

questions.q: Compared with the indication from a surface crack, an indication from a subsurface discontinuity is typically:
options: Sharper and more tightly held
Always circular
Visible only under white light
Broader and less distinct
questions.explanation: Leakage from a subsurface discontinuity spreads out before reaching the surface, so the particles form a wider, fuzzier pattern. Surface cracks give sharp, well-defined lines.

questions.q: A fuzzy indication disappears after the part is demagnetized and re-examined. It was most likely:
options: A fatigue crack
A forging lap
Magnetic writing from contact with another magnetized object
A subsurface inclusion
questions.explanation: Magnetic writing is a local residual field left where the part touched another magnetized object; it disappears after demagnetization and does not return. Relevant discontinuities reappear when the part is magnetized and examined again.

questions.q: A known longitudinal crack in a bar was not detected when the bar was magnetized in a coil. What is the most likely reason?
options: The coil field was parallel to the crack, so little leakage field was produced
Coil fields cannot magnetize steel bars
The particles were too fine
Longitudinal cracks can only be found with prods
questions.explanation: A coil gives a longitudinal field along the bar, parallel to a longitudinal crack. A circular field from a head shot or central conductor is needed to cross it.

questions.q: Particles build up heavily along edges and corners and are held across the whole surface, hiding possible indications. The most likely cause is:
options: Field strength too low
Demagnetization not carried out before the examination
UV-A intensity too high
Field strength too high (over-magnetization)
questions.explanation: An excessive field produces strong leakage at geometric features and a heavy background (furring) that can mask relevant indications. The current should be reduced to the level the procedure specifies.

questions.q: An indication is suspected to be non-relevant because it lies at a sharp change in section. What should the Level II do before classifying it?
options: Record it as a crack without further checks
Ignore it, since geometric indications are always non-relevant
Confirm its cause, for example by removing the particles and re-examining, or by another method, before classifying it
Increase the current until the indication becomes sharper
questions.explanation: Section changes can produce non-relevant indications, but cracks also start at these stress raisers. The cause must be confirmed before an indication is dismissed.

questions.q: Why may parts need to be demagnetized after MT?
options: Residual magnetism can cause arc blow during later welding, hold metal chips during machining or affect nearby instruments
Demagnetization removes the particles from the surface
Residual magnetism makes the part non-ferromagnetic
Demagnetization is needed to verify field strength
questions.explanation: A residual field can interfere with welding, machining, plating, bearing operation and sensitive instruments. Whether demagnetization is required, and to what level, is set by the procedure or specification.

questions.q: Which principle underlies effective demagnetization?
options: Applying a single strong DC pulse in the same direction as the magnetizing field
Warming the part to about 100 °C
Tapping the part with a hammer
Subjecting the part to a field that reverses direction while its strength is gradually reduced to zero
questions.explanation: A reversing field of decreasing strength takes the material round smaller and smaller hysteresis loops until little residual field remains. The starting field should be at least as strong as the field used for the examination.

questions.q: A large part was magnetized with DC. Why might AC demagnetization through a coil leave a residual field?
options: AC does not reverse direction
The AC field is concentrated near the surface by the skin effect and may not reach the deeper magnetized material
AC demagnetization increases retentivity
AC cannot be reduced in strength
questions.explanation: AC demagnetization works well near the surface, but its field does not penetrate deeply. Reversing, stepped-down DC is used where a DC field penetrated deep into a large section.

questions.q: How is the residual field normally checked after demagnetization?
options: With a field indicator or gaussmeter, as the procedure specifies
With a UV-A radiometer
With a settling tube
By measuring the part's temperature
questions.explanation: A field indicator or Hall-effect gaussmeter shows whether the remaining field is within the limit set by the procedure or customer specification.

questions.q: Which is an appropriate safety precaution during MT?
options: Remove a cracked UV-A lamp filter to make the lamp brighter
Energize the prods before they are in firm contact to check the current
Avoid looking directly into the UV-A lamp and keep oil-based suspensions away from ignition sources
Use prods on finished bearing surfaces, since arc strikes are harmless
questions.explanation: UV-A lamps should not be viewed directly, and damaged filters must be replaced because they can pass harmful radiation. Petroleum-based carriers are combustible, and prods must be in firm contact before current flows to avoid arcing.
